headline: Check each display's bins against the commute values
expl: Start by listing which data values fall into each interval of choice A and choice D, then count them and compare the two bar sets. Next, check whether each stemplot in choice B includes every one of the twelve values, using the stem and leaf structure in the stem-and-leaf plot fact.

headline: Compare the sampling plan's steps with the four named random designs
expl: Read the sampling plan and list each step it describes: how the first unit is chosen and how the later units are picked. Then compare that pattern against the definitions of the four random sampling methods in the supplied facts, checking whether each definition's key mechanism appears in the plan. Decide which single design's mechanism the plan matches.

headline: Check what kind of values the model code holds
expl: Read the stem's description of the recorded variable and ask whether its values are category names or numerical measurements. Then compare that with the definitions of categorical and quantitative variables in the supplied facts, and decide which definition the model code fits.

headline: Compare the poll's selection process with the bias types listed in the facts
expl: Read how the website chooses who responds: visitors decide to click on their own. Check the bias-type list in the supplied facts and match the described process to the matching definition, then compare that match against each answer choice's stated reason.

headline: Match each summary value to its box and whisker parts
expl: Read the stem's five-number summary and map each value to the box edges, median line, and whisker ends. Then use the 1.5 × IQR fence rule with the given Q1 and Q3 to decide whether the minimum lies beyond a fence and would be drawn as an outlier.

headline: Compare the blocked design to the completely randomized one
expl: Read the stem's design description and the facts on completely randomized designs and confounding variables. Ask what role sun exposure plays as a variable that could affect yield, and whether the stem's design accounts for it. Then check how each choice describes the effect of that design on variability and on detecting a difference.

headline: Check each description against the five-number summary and the 1.5 x IQR rule
expl: Start by computing the IQR from Q1 and Q3 in the summary, then test the outlier cutoffs using the min and max. Compare the mean with the median to judge skew, and note which features each choice names and whether they match the summary values.

headline: Find each group's quartiles, then compare the two IQRs
expl: Start by ordering each group's data from smallest to largest, since the 9 values are already sorted in the stem. Then locate the median and the medians of the lower and upper halves for each group, and subtract Q1 from Q3 within each group. Finally, subtract Group B's IQR from Group A's, keeping track of the sign.

headline: Find the quartiles of each group's data before comparing their spreads
expl: Sort each group's values and locate Q1 and Q3 using the median-of-halves method for the nine values in each list. Compute each group's IQR as Q3 minus Q1, then subtract Group B's IQR from Group A's, keeping the sign of the result.

headline: Find each group's mean, then take the difference in order
expl: Use the mean formula on each group's list: add all nine heights and divide by 9 for Group A, then do the same for Group B. Subtract Group B's mean from Group A's mean, keeping the sign of the result. Check your sums by counting the values you added.

headline: Compare the p-value to the significance level in choice D
expl: Read the stem's decision question alongside the convention on small versus not-small p-values, and check what the significance level is compared against. Then decide which choice matches the decision rule described in the supplied facts about whether a small p-value gives evidence for Ha.

headline: Compare choice D with what random assignment actually controls
expl: Reread the facts on completely randomized designs and confounding variables. Ask what problem random assignment is meant to solve when comparing treatment groups, then check which choice describes that purpose rather than a side effect.

headline: Read the stem's referent and match the phrase to its meaning
expl: The stem "What does that mean?" refers to a value mentioned in a preceding context you can see in the question data, so first identify what "that" points to. Then compare what each choice says about the score's position among the whole data set, using the fact on how percentile-type statements relate a value to the ordered data.

headline: Compare each choice's bias type with who the sampling frame leaves out
expl: Read the stem's sampling method: residents are called from a landline directory. Ask which group of residents could never be selected by that method, then check the bias definitions in the supplied list of sampling bias types to see which one names that kind of exclusion.

headline: Compare the two group means with their spreads before judging 'always'
expl: Read the stem's two means and the shared SD of about 14 for each group, and ask what a difference of 5 points means when each group's values vary by about 14 points. Then check the claim's word 'always' against that overlap, using the in-context fact that results must be tied to the survey's variables and population.

headline: Check how caffeine was assigned and what else differs between groups
expl: Read the stem and ask whether the researcher imposed caffeine or the students chose it themselves. Then consider whether the group that drinks caffeine also differs on another measurable trait, such as study time, that could affect the outcome. Compare those two features against the definitions of experiment, explanatory variable, and confounding variable.

headline: Compare the two group means using each group's full list of totals
expl: Start by finding each group's mean separately, adding all nine receipt totals in Group A and all nine in Group B and dividing by 9. Then subtract Group B's mean from Group A's mean, keeping track of the sign of the result.

headline: Check the denominator's sign and size as t approaches -1 from the left
expl: Look at the stem's limit: the numerator t^2+3 stays positive near t=-1, while the denominator (t+1)^4 is a fourth power that gets very small as t→-1. Use the facts on unbounded behavior and vertical asymptotes: decide whether the quotient grows without bound, and whether the sign of the result (positive or negative) depends on the side of approach.

headline: Compare the left and right limits at x = 2 using the piecewise rules
expl: Find the limit of f as x approaches 2 from the left by substituting into the x < 2 piece, then find the limit from the right using the x \ge 2 piece. Then compare those two one-sided limits with each other and with f(2), using the discontinuity types in the supplied fact.

headline: Match each summary value to the boxplot part it defines
expl: Read the five-number summary and list which values set the box edges, median line, whisker ends, and plotted points. Use the 1.5 × IQR fence rule with the given whisker endpoints to decide which values fall outside the whiskers and should be drawn as individual points. Check each choice's box, median, whiskers, and outliers against that list.

headline: Factor numerator and denominator of m(x) to inspect shared factors
expl: Start by factoring both the numerator x^2 - 2x and the denominator x^3 - 4x^2 + 4x completely, looking for any factor they share. Then, for each x-value where a factor equals zero, compare what remains after cancelling shared factors with the Types of discontinuities fact, which describes removable discontinuities and vertical-asymptote discontinuities.

headline: Find the limit of f(x) as x approaches 3 using the given facts
expl: Read the definition of continuity at x = c and the fact on removing a discontinuity. Consider what the limit of f(x) as x approaches 3 must equal for f to be continuous there, and consider how factoring the numerator of f(x) might help you evaluate that limit.

headline: Apply the inverse derivative formula at the right input point
expl: Read the inverse-derivative fact and note that it needs f' evaluated at f^{-1}(4), so first find the x-value where f(x) equals 4. Then compute f' at that x using the given f(x) = x³ + 2x + 1, and set up the reciprocal with that value.

headline: Differentiate each term of g(x) using the supplied rules
expl: Read the stem's definition of g(x) and identify each term, then apply the supplied power rule to the x³ term and the constant multiple and difference rules to the -2f(x) term. Once you have the derivative expression for g′(x), substitute x = 4 and use the given value of f′(4).

headline: Factor the denominator and test where it is zero
expl: Vertical asymptotes come from x-values where the denominator is zero but the function is unbounded there, so check each zero of x(x-2)^2 and see whether the numerator cancels it. Compare the factors of the numerator x^2 - 4 with the factors of the denominator, then decide for each candidate whether the limit is infinite or a removable discontinuity.

headline: Check the denominator's sign as x approaches 1 from the left
expl: Factor the denominator x^2 - 2x + 1 and see which value it approaches as x→1, then check the sign of the numerator at x = 1 and of the denominator for x slightly less than 1. Use the unbounded-behavior fact to decide whether the limit is infinite or a finite number, and check the sign of the infinite result from the left.

headline: Set up the inverse derivative formula at x = 10
expl: Before submitting, read the derivative of an inverse function fact and identify what a = 10 stands for, namely which x-value on the original function f gives f(x) = 10. Then compute f'(x) for f(x) = x² + 3x, and use the domain condition x ≥ 0 to decide which solution applies. Work through these steps yourself to reach the value.

headline: Compare the left and right limits at x = 1 using the piecewise rules
expl: Find the value each piece approaches as x nears 1: substitute 1 into the expression for x < 1 and into the expression for x >= 1 separately. Then compare those two results with f(1) and the discontinuity types in the supplied fact.

headline: Pick the table values on each side of x = 8 for a difference quotient
expl: Find the listed x-values just below and just above 8 in the table, then write the difference quotient using those two points: change in f(x) divided by change in x. Use the formula fact about difference quotients to set up the fraction with the correct f-values and x-values, then compare the result to the choices.

headline: Compare the left and right pieces of f at x = 2
expl: Find the value each piece of the definition gives at x = 2: substitute 2 into the x²−1 branch and into the kx+1 branch. Continuity requires the one-sided limits from both sides to match f(2), so set the two expressions equal and solve for k.

headline: Rewrite the tangent using sine and cosine before taking the limit
expl: Read the supplied strategy on alternate trigonometric forms and apply it to tan(2x), which is the denominator in R(x). Look for a rearrangement of 5x/tan(2x) that puts a sine-over-argument pattern in front of the limit, then decide which standard limit that pattern matches.

headline: Check the two one-sided limits at x = -2 against S(-2)
expl: Compare the two pieces of S at x = -2: the first piece x^3 + ax applies at x = -2 (since x <= -2), and the second piece x^2 - a applies just to the right. Use the continuity definition in the supplied fact: the left-hand limit, the right-hand limit, and S(-2) must all match. Write each one-sided limit as an expression in a and set them equal to find the condition on a.

headline: Identify the outer and inner functions of f(x)
expl: Rewrite the square root as a power so the function has a clear outer operation and inner expression. Then use the composite-function chain rule on the inner part, reading the supplied chain rule fact for the pattern to apply.

headline: Factor the denominator and check which x-values make it zero
expl: Read the stated factorization x(x - 2)^2 in the denominator and list every x-value where that denominator equals zero. Then check whether the numerator also cancels each of those factors, using the fact that a limit can be infinite near a point where the function is unbounded.

headline: Track how the average rate changes as h shrinks toward 0
expl: Each table entry is an average rate of change over [1, 1 + h], which matches the difference-quotient form in the first fact. The instantaneous rate at t = 1 is the limit of these quotients as h approaches 0, as the second fact describes. Look at the sequence of values as h gets smaller and decide what number they are approaching.

headline: Identify u(x) and v(x) in g(x) and set up the product rule
expl: Read the product rule fact and split g(x) = (x³ − 4)(2x + 5) into two factors, naming one u(x) and the other v(x). Write down u′(x) and v′(x) from those two factors, then plug x = 1 into each piece in the product rule structure before doing any arithmetic.

headline: Apply limit theorems to the numerator and denominator separately
expl: Read the stem's given limits for u(t) and v(t) at t→6, then identify which combination rules (sums, differences, products, quotients, powers) apply to the numerator (u(t))^2 − 3v(t) and the denominator u(t) + 2v(t). Substitute each given limit value into the pieces you have built up, keeping track of the order of operations, and check that the denominator's limit is nonzero before you finish.

headline: Apply limit rules to each piece of the expression
expl: Read the given limits of S(p) and D(p) at p = 10 and identify which combinations appear in the numerator and denominator. Use the limit theorems for sums, differences, products, powers and quotients to rewrite the limit in terms of those two values, checking that the denominator's limit is not zero before dividing.

headline: Set up the difference quotient using the two given x-values
expl: A secant slope uses the average rate of change formula, which compares the function's outputs at the two endpoints of the interval. Find h(0) and h(3) by substituting each x-value into h(x), then place those outputs and the x-values into the difference quotient $\frac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a}$.

headline: Find dy/dx with the quotient rule, then set it equal to zero
expl: A horizontal tangent occurs where dy/dx equals zero, so first write the derivative of the given function using the quotient rule: the numerator is $v(x)\,u'(x)-u(x)\,v'(x)$ over $[v(x)]^{2}$, with $u=x$ and $v=x^{2}+4$. Simplify the numerator fully, then solve the resulting equation for x and check each solution against the answer choices.

headline: Locate the input 6 in the table and identify what f⁻¹ needs
expl: Start by finding the row where the input to f⁻¹ is 6, meaning the x-value whose f(x) equals 6, then note which column gives the derivative of f at that x. Use the inverse-derivative fact with a=6 and check the condition that the derivative at f⁻¹(6) is nonzero.

headline: Set up the limit of s(x) as x approaches 2 and match it to s(2)
expl: Read the stem's rule for s(x) when x is not 2, and note that continuity at x = 2 requires the limit as x approaches 2 to equal s(2). Apply the fact that removing a discontinuity means the limit value must match the defined value, then work out how the numerator must behave at x = 2 for the limit to be finite.

headline: Apply the chain rule to the arccos derivative with inner function 2x
expl: Identify the outer function arccos(u) and the inner function u = 2x, then read the arccos derivative fact to find the expression evaluated at u. Next, multiply by the derivative of the inner function du/dx, using the chain rule fact.

headline: Factor the denominator and check the sign of each factor near p = -3
expl: Factor p^2 + 5p + 6 and see which factor goes to zero at p = -3 while the numerator stays nonzero. Then decide the sign of each factor for p slightly greater than -3, since the approach is from the right. The fact on unbounded behavior and infinite limits tells you how to interpret what the expression does as the denominator approaches zero.

headline: Inspect the numerator's factoring before evaluating the limit
expl: Read the stem's rational expression and compare its numerator to the denominator x - 3. Use the supplied strategy on algebraic manipulation: consider whether an equivalent form of the expression can be obtained by factoring the numerator and dividing out common factors before substituting x = 3.

headline: Check each choice's domain against the interval [1, 6]
expl: Use the fact that continuity holds at every point of a function's domain, so first find where each expression is defined. For each choice, check whether any x from 1 to 6 makes a denominator zero, a logarithm argument nonpositive, or a square root argument negative.

headline: Apply the chain rule to arcsin of e^x at x = −ln 2
expl: Identify the outer function arcsin(u) and the inner function u = e^x, then write the chain rule as dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx) using the arcsin derivative formula and the derivative of e^x. Substitute x = −ln 2 into the resulting expression, and simplify e^{−ln 2} carefully before comparing with the choices.

headline: Differentiate sec x and cot x separately, then evaluate at π/3
expl: Use the trig derivative formulas for sec x and cot x, which are listed in the derivatives of tan, cot, sec, csc fact, and apply the difference rule to g(x) = sec x − cot x. Then substitute x = π/3 and use the exact values of sec(π/3) and tan(π/3) and csc(π/3) and cot(π/3)? Check which values of cos, sin, sec, and csc you need at π/3 before simplifying.

headline: Read the limit's form and pick the matching algebraic strategy
expl: Look at the stem's expression sin(3x)/x and check the supplied strategy list for the technique that fits a trigonometric expression. Rewrite the expression into an equivalent form that you can evaluate directly as x approaches 0, then substitute carefully.

headline: Set up the inverse-derivative formula for f at x = 10
expl: Read the supplied inverse-derivative formula and identify what a must be here, which is the output value 10 of f. Then find the input x with f(x) = 10 by solving x² + 3x = 10 on the domain x ≥ 0, and compute f′ at that x using the derivative of f.

headline: Differentiate both sides of the implicit equation with respect to x
expl: Start by applying d/dx to every term of sin(xy) + y = π/2, using the product rule inside the sine argument and the chain rule for y, as described in the implicit differentiation fact. Keep track of where dy/dx appears, then collect those terms so you can solve for dy/dx algebraically.

headline: Differentiate both sides of xy² = 18 with respect to x
expl: Start by applying the product rule to the term xy² and the chain rule to any y-terms, using the given equation and the point (2, 3). Then isolate dy/dx and substitute x = 2 and y = 3 to evaluate it.

headline: Check the limit and recorded value separately
expl: Compare the left-hand and right-hand limits at x = 2 and decide whether they match, since that determines whether the two-sided limit exists. Then compare the limit with f(2) to see whether the value at the point agrees with the limit, and check the discontinuity types in the facts against what you find.

headline: Trace which elements each molecule needs from the supplied facts
expl: Read the element-use list and find which molecules it links to each of the elements the question changes. Then compare that list with the element the researcher restored, and trace what each molecule still lacks.

headline: Pick the two table points around x = 4 and set up a difference quotient
expl: Find the two x-values in the table that lie closest to 4, one on each side. Write the difference quotient $\frac{f(x_2)-f(x_1)}{x_2-x_1}$ using those two points, then compute the change in f divided by the change in x.

headline: Rewrite f(x) with a negative exponent, then apply the power rule
expl: Start by rewriting $f(x)=\frac{3}{x^{2}}$ so the variable sits in the numerator with an exponent, using the constant multiple. Then apply the power rule from the supplied fact to the power term, keeping track of the constant and the new exponent. Check that your final expression matches one of the four choices exactly, including the sign.

headline: Compare how fat X and fat Y chains differ in bonding
expl: Read the supplied fact on saturated versus unsaturated fatty acids and note what it says about carbon-carbon bonds. Then use the convention on unsaturation and physical state to connect that chain structure to packing and whether each fat is liquid or solid. Check each choice against that chain-shape idea and reject any that describe the wrong bond type or the wrong effect on shape.

headline: Compare each choice's bonding claim with the water polarity facts
expl: Read the stem's phrase about water absorbing heat with little temperature change, then check each choice against the supplied facts on polarity, hydrogen bonding, and heat-related properties of water. Pay attention to whether each choice names the correct type of bond and whether it links that bond to the heat behavior described.

headline: Compare membrane area and volume between the two cells in the table
expl: Read the surface area and volume columns for the smooth and folded cells, and note which values change and which stay fixed. Then consider how the stated per-area uptake rate and per-volume nutrient requirement apply to each cell's numbers, and check each choice against those comparisons.

headline: Compare the internal membrane areas and enzyme counts in the two cells
expl: Read the stem's internal membrane area values for Cell X and Cell Y, and note that each unit of membrane area carries the same enzyme count. Then check the 'increasing surface area' item in the second fact to see what extra membrane surface provides for reactions, and test each choice against that idea.

headline: Compare the two sugar structures in the answer choices
expl: Start by reading each choice and noting what it claims distinguishes the two sugars. Then check the facts on transport proteins and large polar molecules, and ask what kind of molecular feature a protein binding site could physically recognize.

headline: Compare the temperature effect with the structural change in the stem
expl: Read the stem's sentence about heating disrupting hydrogen bonds and changing the active site's shape, and set it beside the supplied fact on temperature outside an enzyme's optimal range. Then ask what that structural change does to the enzyme's ability to bind substrate, and check each choice against that effect.

headline: Compare how hydrogen bonding affects heat absorption and evaporation
expl: Read the stem's comparison of the replacement liquid with water, focusing on what it says about hydrogen bonds. Then sort out separately what each trial measures: the temperature change in the first trial and the energy drawn from the organism in the second. Use the supplied facts on specific heat capacity and heat of vaporization to decide how each property depends on bonding strength.

headline: Compare each choice's control and the measured variable
expl: Read the stem's treatment, which removes one polysaccharide while leaving the others, and ask which measurement would reflect structural support. Check in each choice whether the control differs from the treatment only in the agent being tested, and whether the response measured connects to structure.

headline: Compare each choice's evidence with what engulfment would predict
expl: Read each choice and ask what observation it describes, then ask whether that observation would show a prokaryote being taken inside a host cell rather than just sharing ancestry. Use the endosymbiosis fact to set what the question is testing: how a prokaryote came to sit inside a host.

reason: The hint mentions 'heat of vaporization', a term that does not appear in the question stem. Since choice D is the only option that includes heat of vaporization, introducing this specific property directly points the student to the correct choice.
headline: Match each phenomenon in the stem to a supplied fact before comparing choices
expl: Read the two phenomena in the stem and find which supplied fact about water's energy behavior and which fact about hydrogen-bond-based properties each one connects to. Before choosing, state each matched fact in your own words and check which choice pairs the right property with each phenomenon.

reason: The hint states that 'information is encoded in the sequence of nucleotides', which directly gives away the core concept and phrasing of the correct answer choice (B).
headline: Reread the Components of a nucleotide fact and list what the segments share
expl: Look at the stem and identify exactly what the two segments are said to have in common and what is said to differ. Then reread the supplied fact on the components of a nucleotide and state in your own words what a nucleotide is built from. Compare those two lists against each choice before deciding.

headline: Read the residual plot pattern against the model's fit
expl: Start with the residual definition: each residual is actual minus predicted, plotted against the input. Then check what a good residual plot looks like (no pattern) and compare the U-shape you see with that standard to judge what the model is doing across the input interval.

headline: Compare how each choice describes water in breaking bonds
expl: Read the stem's description of breaking covalent bonds between subunits, then look at the supplied hydrolysis fact and note what happens to water in that reaction. Check each choice for whether it matches that water direction and whether it describes breaking or forming bonds. Decide which choice fits both parts.

headline: Swap x and y in y = 5^x, then solve for y
expl: Rewrite f(x) = 5^x as y = 5^x, then interchange x and y to get x = 5^y. Use the definition of a logarithm in the supplied facts to isolate y, reading the base carefully as you do so. Compare your solved expression with the four choices.

headline: Substitute a variable for e^x and factor the quadratic
expl: Rewrite e^(2x) using the power property for exponents as (e^x)^2, which turns the equation into a quadratic in e^x. Factor that quadratic and then check each factor's solution against the rule that e^x is always positive before solving for x with the definition of a logarithm.

headline: Compare the data's differences and ratios across the table
expl: Compute the first differences and the successive ratios of the five y-values, then compute the second differences if needed. Use the convention that the most appropriate model depends on the pattern you observe and on context, and check which pattern your calculations actually show.

headline: Compare each zero's multiplicity with the even-multiplicity fact
expl: Read the stem's multiplicity for each zero, then check the even-multiplicity convention to see how it affects the graph at that zero. Apply that check to −1 and to 3 separately before comparing your findings with the four choices.

headline: Isolate the logarithm in the regression equation and set y equal to 12
expl: Start by substituting y = 12 into the given model y = 4.8 + 2.3 ln(x), then isolate the ln(x) term by undoing the addition and the multiplication by 2.3. Once you have ln(x) alone, use the definition of a logarithm (with ln meaning base e) to rewrite the equation in exponential form, which turns the problem into finding x as a power of e.

headline: Restrict the domain, then swap x and y to find the inverse
expl: Read the stem's domain restriction x ≤ 2 and the vertex form of f. Check whether f is one-to-one on that domain, using the fact that an inverse is built by reversing input-output pairs. Then reverse the roles of x and y in y = (x−2)²+3, solve for y, and keep the sign and domain that match the restricted domain of f.

headline: Relate the period to the 4-cycles-in-24-seconds data
expl: Start by reading the stem's statement of 4 full cycles over 24 seconds and decide what length of input interval corresponds to one full cycle. Then look at the period fact and the general form y = a*sin(b(x+c)) + d, and consider how the period of such a function is related to b. Work out your own relationship between the period and b before choosing among the choices.

headline: Find the endpoints of the segment from x = 2 to x = 5
expl: Read the two points of the graph at x = 2 and x = 5 from the stated vertices. Then apply the average rate of change formula, the change in output divided by the change in input, to those two points. Compare the sign and size of your result with each choice's direction and value.

headline: Compare consecutive outputs and check whether the differences or ratios repeat
expl: Start by listing the outputs for x = 0, 1, 2, 3 and finding the change from each output to the next. Use the convention that equal-length input steps with constant additive change signal a linear function, while constant proportional change signals an exponential one. Then check whether each step produces the same difference or the same ratio, and compare that result with the reasoning in each choice.

headline: Apply the polar-to-rectangular formulas to r and θ
expl: Read the stem's values r = -4 and θ = π/3 and substitute them into x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ from the polar-to-rectangular conversion fact. Evaluate cos(π/3) and sin(π/3) from the unit circle, keeping the sign of r in each product, then match the resulting pair to a choice.

headline: Combine the two logarithms using the product property
expl: Read the stem's equation and note both logarithms share base 3, so they can be merged into one logarithm of a single expression. Then use the definition of a logarithm to rewrite the equation in exponential form, and check any candidate against the domain restriction that arguments of logarithms must be positive.

headline: Factor the numerator and compare it with the denominator
expl: Read the stem's function h(x)=(x²−9)/(x−3) and factor the numerator as a difference of squares. Then check which factors cancel and which remain in the denominator, using the supplied hole and vertical asymptote conditions on the zeros and their multiplicities.

headline: Use the average rate of change formula on the cubic model
expl: Read the question's model y=0.42x³−1.8x²+0.65x+7.1 and the interval from x=2.4 to x=3.1. The change in predicted y over an interval divided by the interval length is the average rate of change, so set up that quotient with f(3.1) and f(2.4) substituted into the given cubic. Evaluate each cubic value carefully, subtract, and keep the rounding instruction in mind for the final form.

headline: Compare the stem's third and second differences to the degree pattern
expl: Read the stem's clue about which difference stays constant, and connect it to the facts on degree and leading term. Think about how the order of the first difference that becomes constant relates to the polynomial's degree, then match that to the choices.

headline: Rewrite 1/8 as a power of 4 using the logarithm definition
expl: Start from the definition $\log_b c = a \iff b^{a} = c$ and set $b=4$, $c=\frac{1}{8}$, so you need to find $a$ with $4^{a}=\frac{1}{8}$. Notice that both 4 and 8 are powers of 2, so try writing each as $2^{n}$ and compare the exponents.

headline: Compare how h changes as t doubles, using the table's input and output pairs
expl: Look at the input values 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and note how each one is multiplied by 2 from row to row. Then compare the matching changes in h: decide whether the outputs change by equal additive steps or by equal multiplicative steps, and match that pattern to the growth-type comparison in the supplied fact on exponential versus logarithmic growth.

headline: Set up the division of p(x) by x−2 using the remainder theorem
expl: Start by identifying the value of x that makes the divisor x−2 equal to zero, since that is the input the remainder theorem asks you to evaluate. Then substitute that value into the standard-form polynomial p(x)=a_n x^n+...+a_0 from the supplied formula, working carefully with each coefficient and sign. Compare your result with the four answer choices once you have carried out the substitution yourself.

headline: Match the slope to the log form of y = ab^x
expl: Take the base-10 logarithm of both sides of y = ab^x, then rewrite the result as a linear equation in x. Compare that linear form's slope with the given slope 0.3010 to find what quantity equals it. The semi-log linearization fact lists the slope in terms of the base of the logarithm and b.

headline: Rewrite the exponent 3x−1 as a product of separate exponents
expl: Read the stem's expression 5·2^(3x−1) and the power-property fact on exponents of the form b^{cx}, along with the product-property fact for splitting a sum in an exponent. Use the product property to split 3x−1 into two separate exponent terms, then look at how the base 2 appears in each term and what the multiplied constant becomes. Compare the resulting form with each choice's constant and base.

headline: Compare the crucible masses across heating cycles to find the stable mass
expl: Read the three post-heating masses and decide which pair shows the sample has reached constant mass, since water loss stops once that happens. Then subtract the empty crucible mass from the damp-sample mass to get the starting sample mass, and the lost mass comes from the damp-sample reading minus the final stable reading. Use these two masses in a percent-by-mass setup, and check each answer choice against what your numbers can actually support.

headline: Count the valence electrons in OH⁻ before comparing the four diagrams
expl: Start with the fact that lists the principles for building a Lewis diagram, and use its first item to total the electrons for O, H and the extra negative charge. Then check each choice's bonds and lone pairs against that total, counting two electrons per lone pair and making sure each atom's electrons add up correctly.

headline: Set up the moles of solute before and after dilution
